lessons.title: Getting Started with ArkTS
lessons.summary: What ArkTS is, why HarmonyOS prefers it, and the four pillars that separate it from TypeScript.

content.text: ArkTS is the preferred programming language for HarmonyOS application development. Built on the TypeScript ecosystem, it keeps the familiar TS style while extending the language with stronger static checks for stability and performance.
Since API version 10, ArkTS further strengthens static check and analysis. Understanding these pillars early will make every later lesson clearer.

items: Forced static types — every value has a definite compile-time type; no any.
Forbidden runtime object-layout changes — properties cannot be added/removed dynamically.
Restricted operator semantics — e.g. unary + only on numbers.
No structural typing — types match by declared identity (classes/interfaces), not by shape alone.

content.title: How this course maps to official docs
content.text: Lessons follow Huawei’s Learning ArkTS pathway: Introduction → Coding Style → Migration Background → TypeScript to ArkTS Cookbook → Adaptation Cases → High-Performance Programming. Each lesson links to the matching official page.
ArkTS remains compatible with the TypeScript and JavaScript ecosystem. You can write new ArkTS code or reuse existing TS/JS where the runtime allows — covered later in Migration Background.

lessons.title: Basics: Declarations & Types
lessons.summary: let/const, number, string, boolean, arrays, enums, unions, and type aliases from Introduction to ArkTS.
lessons.sourceLabel: Official: Introduction to ArkTS — The Basics

content.text: let introduces a variable that may be reassigned. const introduces a read-only constant that can be assigned only once. Prefer const by default.

content.code:
let hi: string = 'hello'
hi = 'hello, world'

const greeting: string = 'hello'
content.title: let-const

content.text: If an initializer is present, ArkTS can often infer the type. Both of these are string:

content.code:
let hi1: string = 'hello'
let hi2 = 'hello, world'
content.title: inference

items: number — integers and floats (decimal, hex 0x, octal 0o, binary 0b)
bigint — for integers beyond safe number precision
boolean — true / false
string — quotes or template literals with backticks and ${expression}
void — function returns nothing
Object / object — base reference types
T[] — arrays of element type T
enum — named value sets
union — T | U combinations
type aliases — name complex types

content.title: Basic vs reference
content.text: number and string behave as basic values. Objects, arrays, and functions are reference types — assigning them copies the reference, not a deep clone.

content.code:

let c: ColorSet = ColorSet.Red

type Id = number | string
let id: Id = 42
id = 'user-1'

lessons.title: Interfaces, Generics & Null Safety
lessons.summary: Interfaces, generics, non-null by default, ??, optional chaining, and modules overview.
lessons.sourceLabel: Official: Introduction to ArkTS — Interface / Null Safety

content.text: An interface describes a contract of properties and methods. Classes implement interfaces. Interfaces can extend other interfaces.

content.title: interface

content.text: Generic classes, interfaces, and functions parameterize types. Constraints use extends. Prefer explicit type arguments when inference is limited (ArkTS rule).

content.title: generic

content.text: Types are non-nullable by default. null must be opt-in via T | null. Use ?? for defaults and ?. for optional chaining.

content.code:
let x: number | null = null
x = 1
const nick: string | null = null
const display: string = nick ?? ''
content.title: null-safety
Modules (overview)
content.text: Use export / import to share types and functions across .ets files. Top-level statements and this-binding rules are stricter than loose JS modules.

lessons.title: Coding Style: Naming & Format
lessons.summary: UpperCamelCase, lowerCamelCase, CONSTANT_CASE, boolean names, braces, and line length.

content.text: The ArkTS Coding Style Guide improves standardization, security, and performance. Rules must be followed; recommendations should be considered.

items: Classes, enums, namespaces → UpperCamelCase (Person, UserType)
Variables, methods, parameters → lowerCamelCase (userName, sendMsg)
Constants & enum values → UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_USER_SIZE)
Booleans → positive names with is/has/can/should (avoid isNotError)
Clear English intent — no Pinyin, no cryptic single letters (except loop indices)

content.title: naming

items: Spaces for indentation
≤ 120 characters per line
Always use braces for if/else and loops
Prefer single quotes for strings in style guide samples
Object literals with >4 properties: one property per line
Put else/catch on the same line as the closing brace

lessons.title: Coding Style: Programming Practices
lessons.summary: Access modifiers, NaN checks, array methods, finally rules, avoid ESObject, prefer T[].
lessons.sourceLabel: Official: ArkTS Coding Style Guide — Practices

content.text: Add public / private / protected so intent is explicit for readers and tooling.

items: Write 0.5 not .5; write 1.0 not 1.
Use Number.isNaN() to test NaN — never x === NaN
Prefer array methods for traversal when appropriate
Declare arrays as T[] (e.g. number[]) rather than Array alone
Do not assign inside control conditions (if (x = y))
Do not return/break/continue/throw from finally

content.title: Avoid ESObject
content.text: ESObject is for ArkTS ↔ JS/TS cross-language boundaries. Using it elsewhere forces expensive cross-language calls. Prefer native ArkTS types.

lessons.title: Migration Background
lessons.summary: Why ArkTS tightens TypeScript: stability, performance, .ets compatibility, and TS/JS interop.

content.text: Building on TypeScript syntax, ArkTS strengthens static checks so more errors are caught during development — improving stability and runtime performance.

Dynamic languages can hide undefined bugs until runtime. TS helps with annotations, but optional typing still leaves gaps. ArkTS forces a static type system and stricter checks, including explicit field initialization.

content.title: explicit-init
content.caption: Uninitialized fields that can be undefined are a common TS footgun.

content.text: JS engines must keep runtime type checks. ArkTS compiles to Ark bytecode with known layouts, enabling ahead-of-time optimization and fewer runtime checks.

items: .ets code compatibility — ArkTS files use the .ets extension
Interaction with TS/JS — interop is supported with clear boundaries
ArkCompiler runtime compatibility with TS/JS modules

lessons.title: TS→ArkTS: Core Restrictions
lessons.summary: Static typing, no any/unknown, let not var, fixed object layout, restricted operators, no structural typing.
lessons.sourceLabel: Official: TypeScript to ArkTS Migration Guide

content.text: ArkTS constrains TS features that hurt correctness or force runtime overhead. Code rewritten to these rules remains valid TypeScript.
Ban any and unknown. Model API results with explicit classes/interfaces instead of untyped bags of data.

content.title: no-any

content.text: 2. Object layout cannot change at runtime

items: No adding/removing properties dynamically
No delete operator
No indexed field access for arbitrary keys (obj[field])
No Symbol()-generated keys

content.text: Unary +, -, ~ apply to numbers only — no implicit string-to-number coercion.
Two types are not interchangeable just because they share the same fields. Use explicit inheritance, interfaces, or aliases.

content.title: Constraint levels
content.text: Error = compile fails. Warning = compiles now but may become an error later. Treat warnings as errors in new code.

lessons.title: TS→ArkTS: Everyday Recipes
lessons.summary: Practical cookbook rules: casting, destructuring, throw, for-in, nested functions, and more.
lessons.sourceLabel: Official: TypeScript to ArkTS Cookbook — Recipes

items: Use private keyword — not #fields
Cast only with as T — not angle-bracket casts
No destructuring assignments/declarations/params — use temp variables
No for...in — use indexed for on arrays
No nested function declarations — use arrow functions
throw only Error instances
No delete, no in operator, limited typeof/instanceof
No JSX
Arrow functions instead of function expressions
Declare class fields in the class body — not constructor parameter properties

content.title: no-destructure

lessons.title: High-Performance Programming
lessons.summary: const, stable number kinds, loop hoisting, parameter passing, TypedArray tips, avoid sparse/union arrays & hot exceptions.

content.text: These practices come from real performance-sensitive HarmonyOS code. Apply them in hot paths; combine with the Coding Style Guide for everyday quality.

items: Use const for values that never change
Do not mix ints and floats in the same number variable after init
Avoid arithmetic overflow past INT32 ranges in hot math
Hoist loop-invariant property access outside loops

content.title: hoist

items: Pass external values as parameters instead of capturing heavy closures
Avoid optional parameters in hot functions — use defaults instead
Prefer TypedArray for pure numeric workloads
Avoid sparse arrays (huge length holes → hash storage)
Avoid union arrays like (number | string)[]; keep homogeneous arrays
Do not mix int/float in the same number[] when avoidable

content.text: Creating exceptions builds stack frames. Do not throw inside tight loops — validate once and branch instead.

content.title: Measure what matters
content.text: Micro-optimizations help hottest paths. Clear types and stable layouts already buy most of ArkTS’s performance story.

examples.title: const + hoist
examples.explanation: Cache invariant before looping.

declare function print(arg: any): any

const factor: number = 3
let total: number = 0
for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
  total += i * factor
}
print(total)

courses.title: HarmonyOS Kits
courses.subtitle: Learn HarmonyOS Next system kits — Location, Network, Ability, Data, Media, Camera and Notification.
courses.description: Kit courses teach system capabilities such as location, networking, app abilities, data persistence, media, camera and notifications. Lessons focus on architecture, permissions, and API patterns with copy-ready .ets samples. Practice questions check concepts (permission names, API choices). Device features require DevEco on a device or emulator — not the in-browser ArkTS runner.
learningOutcomes: Explain what a HarmonyOS Kit is and how it fits an application
Identify the import module and key permission for each kit
Recognize core APIs and typical call flow per kit
Choose the right kit for networking, data, media, camera and notifications
Know what belongs in DevEco vs this document-first course

lessons.title: Location Kit overview
lessons.summary: What Location Kit provides and how kits fit HarmonyOS Next apps.

content.text: HarmonyOS Next exposes device and system capabilities through Kits — modular API sets such as Location Kit, Network Kit, and Camera Kit. Your app imports the kit module, declares permissions, then calls typed ArkTS APIs.

items: Obtain the device’s current location (GNSS / network fusion depending on device)
Listen for location updates
Support map and navigation scenarios when combined with Map Kit
Require explicit user-facing permissions and privacy disclosures

content.title: Playground limit
content.text: The in-browser runner cannot access GPS hardware. Use examples as reference code for DevEco Studio; quizzes here ask you to print the correct concept or API name.

// Then request permissions and call location APIs in an Ability / page.

content.text: Location is sensitive personal data. HarmonyOS requires declared permissions in module.json5 (or the project config) and a runtime request with a clear purpose string.

Background location needs additional capability and stronger justification

lessons.title: Ability Kit
lessons.summary: UIAbility, application context, and Want-based navigation.

content.text: The building block of an app
Ability Kit defines UIAbility — the entry component that hosts your pages and owns the application lifecycle. A Want is the message used to start an ability or navigate between abilities and apps.

items: Import: import { UIAbility, Want } from '@kit.AbilityKit'
EntryAbility extends UIAbility and implements onCreate / onWindowStageCreate
Use context.startAbility(want) to launch another ability
AbilityStage and context provide app-level resources

content.title: start-ability
content.caption: Illustrative — field names depend on API version.

content.title: Mental model
content.text: UIAbility ≈ the app entry + lifecycle owner. Want ≈ the intent/message that says which ability to open and what data to pass.

lessons.title: ArkData (Preferences)
lessons.summary: Lightweight key-value persistence for settings and small data.

content.text: ArkData groups the data-management APIs. For simple key-value settings, use Preferences; for structured, queryable data use the Relational Store (RDB). This lesson focuses on Preferences.

items: Import: import { preferences } from '@kit.ArkData'
Best for flags, tokens, and small user settings
Not a database — use RDB for large or relational data

content.title: preferences
content.caption: Reference only — call flush() to persist changes.

content.title: Remember
content.text: Changes are in-memory until flush(); forgetting flush() loses data on restart.

lessons.title: Media Kit
lessons.summary: Play audio and video with AVPlayer.

content.text: Media Kit provides audio and video playback and recording. AVPlayer is the common entry point for streaming or local playback with a state-machine driven lifecycle.

items: Import: import { media } from '@kit.MediaKit'
Create an AVPlayer, set the source url/fd, then prepare and play
React to state changes (initialized, prepared, playing, paused, completed)
Release the player when done to free resources

content.title: avplayer
content.caption: Illustrative — always release the player to avoid leaks.

content.title: Lifecycle
content.text: AVPlayer is state-driven: set the source, wait for initialized/prepared, then play. Skipping states causes errors.

lessons.title: Camera Kit
lessons.summary: Capture photos/video; the CAMERA permission and session flow.

content.text: Camera Kit gives low-level control over camera devices, preview, photo and video capture through a capture session. It requires an explicit runtime permission.

items: Import: import { camera } from '@kit.CameraKit'
Permission: ohos.permission.CAMERA (and MICROPHONE for video with audio)
Flow: get camera manager → create session → add input/output → start
Prefer a higher-level picker when you only need a single photo

content.title: camera-manager
content.caption: Reference only — full capture needs a session and surface in DevEco.

content.title: Privacy
content.text: Camera and microphone are sensitive. Request permission with a clear reason and release the session when the screen closes.

lessons.title: Notification Kit
lessons.summary: Publish local notifications with notificationManager.

content.text: Notification Kit publishes local notifications — text, progress, and rich content — through notificationManager. Remote push is handled separately by Push Kit.

items: Import: import { notificationManager } from '@kit.NotificationKit'
Build a NotificationRequest with an id and content type
Call notificationManager.publish(request)
Users can disable notifications — never assume delivery

content.title: publish
content.caption: Illustrative — field names depend on API version.

content.title: Local vs remote
content.text: Notification Kit = local notifications from your app. Push Kit = messages delivered from a server through Huawei Push.
